usage: The standard toast as everyone raises glasses
More casual/cute; the onomatopoeia of glasses clinking
Formal toast, often led by the boss after a short speech
'One shot' — drink the whole glass in one go (English loan)
examples: 자, 다 같이 건배!
Okay, everyone, cheers!
자 ('alright') gathers attention right before the toast; the whole table echoes 건배! together

A: 오늘 고생하셨습니다. 자, 건배!
B: 건배!

A: You all worked hard today — cheers!
B: Cheers!
A short line of appreciation from the senior precedes the toast; everyone echoes
팀장님이 건배 제의 하셨어요.
The team leader proposed a toast.
건배 제의(를) 하다 = 'to propose a toast'; only the most senior person at the table usually does this
nuance: 건배 is Sino-Korean 乾杯 (literally 'dry the cup'), the all-purpose 'cheers' you say while clinking glasses at the start of drinking. In a 회식 (company dinner) the most senior person says a few words and then leads it, and everyone echoes 건배! in unison. The casual cousin is 짠 (the clink sound), natural among friends or younger coworkers; the formal cousin is 위하여! ('for the sake of ~'), shouted after a stated reason: 우리 팀의 발전을 위하여! ('to our team's growth'). Crucially, 건배 does NOT obligate you to empty the glass — it just means 'cheers'. 원샷 ('one shot') is the separate phrase ordering everyone to down it in one gulp; mixing them up can pressure people to chug when you only meant to toast. The English-speaker pitfall is often the posture, not the word: with a senior present you hold your glass slightly LOWER than theirs when clinking and often turn your head slightly away while drinking — saying 건배 perfectly but clinking above the boss's glass reads as rude. 건배 is a set expression; do not attach particles or split it.

structuredNuance.t: 건배 is Sino-Korean 乾杯, literally 'dry the cup'. The real meaning is simply 'cheers' — a toast said while clinking glasses. It does NOT tell anyone to empty their glass; it is purely a social flourish to mark the start of drinking.

건배 is neutral-register and suits 반말 through 존댓말 tables alike because it is a shouted-together word, not addressed to one person. At a 회식 the senior leads; among friends anyone can call it. 짠 is the warmer, cuter version between close peers; 위하여 is the formal, speech-paired version at official dinners.

건배 (general cheers) vs 짠 (onomatopoeia clink, very casual) vs 위하여 (formal toast following a stated reason) vs 원샷 (orders everyone to down the entire glass). Confusing 건배 with 원샷 is the most common error — 건배 is about clinking, 원샷 is about emptying.
건배 is Sino-Korean 乾杯 ('dry cup'), the same character set as Japanese 乾杯 (kanpai) and Chinese 干杯 (gānbēi). The shared root helps intermediate learners remember it.

The trap is the clinking posture: hold your glass below a senior's when touching glasses, and turn your head slightly away while drinking — saying 건배 correctly but holding your glass higher than the boss's reads as disrespectful. Also, 건배 is a standalone exclamation; do not attach particles (건배를, 건배에) in the toast itself.

mistakes: Saying 원샷! when you just mean 'cheers'.
원샷 orders everyone to empty the glass in one gulp. If you only mean to toast, say 건배!; save 원샷 for when you actually intend to down it.
Clinking your glass above a senior's glass.
The word 건배 is fine, but with elders/bosses you lower your glass below theirs when clinking. Holding yours higher looks disrespectful regardless of the words.
Writing it as 건배에 or 건배를 in the toast.
As a shouted toast it stands alone: 건배! You don't attach particles. 건배를 제의하다 only appears in the longer phrase 'to propose a toast'.

usage: Polite; asking the server or your neighbor to pour
반말, to a close coworker or friend
Let me pour you one more
Offering to fill SOMEONE ELSE'S glass (honorific)
examples: 여기 소주 한 잔 더 주세요.
One more glass of soju here, please.
Naming the drink (소주) makes the order clear to staff; at a 포차 you can also say 한 병 더 (one more bottle)

A: 잔 비었네요. 한 잔 더 드릴까요?
B: 네, 한 잔 더 주세요. 감사합니다.

A: Your glass is empty — can I pour you another?
B: Yes, one more please — thank you.
The full A/B exchange at a typical 회식: A notices the empty glass, B accepts politely
저 한 잔만 더 하고 일어날게요.
I'll have just one more and then head out.
일어나다 ('to get up/leave') politely signals you'll leave soon; 딱 한 잔만 더 makes the limit even firmer
nuance: 한 잔 더 is 한 ('one', native number) + 잔 (counter for cups/glasses) + 더 ('more'), the core phrase for another round. Crucially the counter 잔 takes NATIVE numbers (한, 두, 세 잔), never Sino-Korean (일, 이, 삼) — saying 이 잔 더 instead of 두 잔 더 is a constant learner slip. Watch the direction of the favor verb: 주세요 ('please give') asks someone to pour FOR YOU, while 받으세요 ('please receive') is what you say while pouring for THEM — mixing these completely reverses who is serving whom. The near-synonym 한 잔 더 할게요 uses 하다 ('to do/have a drink') to announce you'll have another yourself, vs. 주세요 which requests it from someone else. Korean pouring culture means you generally don't refill your OWN glass at the table — you pour for others and wait for them to pour for you — so loudly asking 한 잔 더 주세요 while topping up only yourself can look slightly off. Better to offer 한 잔 더 받으세요 to your neighbor first. With a senior pouring for you, receive with two hands and a slight bow.

structuredNuance.t: 한 잔 더 = one(native) + glass(counter) + more. The phrase is literal and transparent, but the cultural meaning is the request within a shared-pouring system: you are asking someone else to pour for you, not grabbing the bottle yourself.

주세요 is polite-neutral and safe for servers, coworkers, or seniors. Drop to 줘 with friends. To offer rather than ask, flip to 받으세요 (polite) or 받아 (casual). Use 주세요 to staff and 받으세요 / 따라 드릴게요 for the person sitting next to you.

한 잔 더 주세요 (ask someone to pour for you) vs 한 잔 더 받으세요 (offer to pour for them) vs 한 잔 더 할게요 (announce you'll have one more yourself). These three are easy to mix up; the verb direction tells you whose glass is being filled.
Scale up: 두 잔 더 주세요 (two more), 한 병 더 주세요 (one more bottle). Scale down: 조금만 더 주세요 (just a little more). Limit: 딱 한 잔만 더 할게요 (exactly one more and that's it).

Two traps: (1) using Sino-Korean numbers with 잔 — 이 잔 대신 두 잔, 삼 잔 대신 세 잔; (2) flipping 주다 and 받다 — 받으세요 is what you say to THEM while pouring into their glass, not what you say when you want a refill yourself.

mistakes: Using Sino-Korean numbers with 잔: 이 잔 더.
잔 takes native numbers. 'Two more glasses' is 두 잔 더, not 이 잔 더. One is 한 잔, two 두 잔, three 세 잔.
Saying 받으세요 when you want them to pour for you.
받으세요 ('please receive') is for when YOU pour into their glass. To ask them to pour for you, say 한 잔 더 주세요 (주다 = give).
Pouring your own glass and announcing 한 잔 더.
Korean drinking custom is to fill others' glasses, not your own. Offer 받으세요 to a neighbor or let someone pour for you, rather than topping up yourself.

english: Let me pour you a drink
usage: Let me pour you a glass
Polite-humble; offering to pour for a senior
반말, to a friend or close junior
Allow me to pour you one (formal)
Very deferential, to a boss/elder at a formal table
Short prompt as you tilt the bottle toward their glass
examples: 부장님, 제가 한 잔 따라 드릴게요.
Director, let me pour you a glass.
Address the senior by title first, then offer; this is the model 회식 junior-to-senior move

A: 잔 비셨네요.
B: 아, 제가 따라 드릴게요.

A: Your glass is empty.
B: Oh, let me pour for you.
B catches the empty glass and offers immediately — the attentive-junior show
두 손으로 따라 드리는 게 예의예요.
Pouring with both hands is the polite way.
두 손으로 ('with both hands') is essential toward elders; right hand on bottle, left supporting the forearm
nuance: 제가 한 잔 따라 드릴게요 breaks down as 제가 ('I', humble subject) + 한 잔 ('one glass') + 따르다 ('to pour') + 드리다 (humble 'give', elevating the receiver) + -ㄹ게요 ('I'll ~'). The verb 따르다 means 'to pour' and is a 르-irregular: 따라, not 따르어. The honorific chain is the whole point: use 드리다 (humble-give) with seniors, plain 주다 (→ 따라 줄게) with peers and juniors. The most formal upgrade is 한 잔 올리겠습니다 (올리다= 'raise/offer upward'), reserved for very senior figures. Do not confuse 따르다 ('to pour') with 따르다 ('to follow') — same spelling; drinking context (bottle + glass) makes the meaning 'pour'. A key cultural note: pouring your OWN glass is avoided; you pour for the person next to you, and they pour for you. Both-hands etiquette: hold the bottle with your right hand and support your right forearm with your left; over-filling to the brim is considered less polished — 80–90% is ideal. Saying 제가 따라 드릴게요 is THE phrase that marks you as socially aware at a Korean table.

structuredNuance.t: 제가 한 잔 따라 드릴게요 = 'I (humble) will pour one glass (for you, humbly)'. The humble double-marker 제가 + 드리다 together signal you are serving someone of higher status. Strip those out for peers: 한 잔 따라 줄게.

Use 따라 드릴게요 with seniors (boss, elder, professor). Use 따라 줄게요 with coworkers/peers. Use 따라 줄게 in casual 반말. Upgrade to 한 잔 올리겠습니다 for very deferential formal occasions. Never pour for yourself at the table — always pour for the person beside you.

따라 드릴게요 (polite offer to pour) vs 받으세요 (short prompt said while actually tipping the bottle) vs 한 잔 올리겠습니다 (most deferential form). 받으세요 tends to accompany the action; 따라 드릴게요 announces the intention first.
따르다 is a 르-irregular: 따라요 (present polite), 따라 드릴게요 (future polite humble), 따라 줄게 (casual). The common slip is 따르어요 — wrong; it must be 따라요.

Two pitfalls: (1) using 줄게요 instead of 드릴게요 for a senior — 따라 줄게요 sounds too flat with a boss; (2) forgetting both-hands etiquette — pouring one-handed toward an elder looks careless. Also, over-filling a glass past 90% is seen as less polished.

mistakes: Using 주다 instead of 드리다 to a senior.
따라 줄게요 is too casual/flat for a boss. The humble 드리다 shows respect: 제가 한 잔 따라 드릴게요. Use 줄게 only with friends/juniors.
Pouring with one hand to an elder.
Toward seniors, pour with both hands (right hand on the bottle, left supporting). One-handed pouring is fine only among close peers/juniors.
Conjugating 따르다 as 따르어/따르어요.
따르다 is a 르-irregular: 따라요, 따라 드릴게요 — not 따르어요. The 르 drops and -아 is added.

english: Your glass is empty — here, let me pour you one
usage: Your glass is empty — have one
Polite; noticing and offering to refill a senior
Your glass is empty — take one
Please allow me to pour you one
Please top up my glass too
채우다 ('to fill'); inviting them to pour back
examples: 부장님, 잔 비었네요. 한 잔 받으세요.
Director, your glass is empty — let me pour you one.
Spot the empty glass and offer; the junior's job at 회식 is to monitor the senior's glass

A: 어, 잔 비었네. 내가 한 잔 따라 줄게.
B: 아, 고마워. 나도 줄까?

A: Oh, your glass is empty — I'll pour you one.
B: Thanks. Want me to pour you one too?
Peer exchange: offering and reciprocating naturally
계속 비어 있길래 한 잔 채워 드렸어요.
It was sitting empty, so I filled it up for you.
-길래 ('since I noticed that') explains why you poured without being asked; 채우다 emphasizes filling to a level
nuance: 잔 비었네요 is 잔 ('glass') + 비다 ('to be empty') in past form 비었- + -네요 (a noticing/remarking ender), meaning 'oh, your glass is empty' — the observation that triggers a refill. You then say 한 잔 받으세요 (받다 'receive' + honorific 으세요), literally 'please receive one', the set phrase said WHILE pouring. This sequence is core 회식 etiquette: watch others' glasses, and when one empties, offer to fill it — you do NOT just refill your own. The verb direction is the main trap: 받으세요 ('please receive') goes with pouring INTO their glass; 주세요 ('please give') is when you want THEM to pour for YOU — beginners flip these and accidentally ask to be poured for instead of offering. 비다 is intransitive ('to be/become empty'), so it's 잔이 비다, not 잔을 비우다 (transitive 비우다 = 'to empty/drain', as in 잔을 비우다 = 'drink the glass dry', a more forceful 'bottoms up' implication). When the senior pours back for you in return, receive with two hands and a slight bow.

structuredNuance.t: 잔 비었네요 = 'The glass has become empty (I notice)'. 한 잔 받으세요 = 'Please receive one glass'. Together they form a paired observation-plus-offer, the most natural way to refill someone's glass at a Korean table. The remark by itself without the offer sounds incomplete.

잔 비었네요, 한 잔 받으세요 is polite-neutral and the standard move junior-to-senior. With peers/friends: 잔 비었다, 받아. To be more deferential to the boss: 한 잔 받으시죠. This sequence happens THROUGHOUT the meal; attentiveness to empty glasses is a social skill.

비다 (intransitive, 'become empty' — state) vs 비우다 (transitive, 'to empty/drain' — action). 잔 비었네요 = the glass IS empty; 잔 비우세요 = drain/finish your glass (more pressure). 받으세요 (you pour into their glass) vs 주세요 (ask them to pour into yours) — never flip these.
More deferential: 한 잔 받으시죠 (-시죠 = polite suggestion). Add 제가: 제가 한 잔 드릴게요. Casual: 한 잔 받아. If they decline: 괜찮으세요? 조금만요?

The classic error is saying 주세요 ('give me') when you mean to OFFER a pour. 받으세요 is what you say to THEM as you tilt the bottle toward their glass; 주세요 is what you say when you want THEM to fill YOUR glass. Also, don't just note the empty glass and do nothing — in Korean drinking culture the observation is implicitly an offer.

mistakes: Saying 주세요 when you're the one pouring for them.
받으세요 ('please receive') goes with pouring into their glass; 주세요 ('please give') asks them to pour for you. Offering a refill is 한 잔 받으세요, not 주세요.
Confusing 잔이 비다 (be empty) with 잔을 비우다 (drain it).
비다 = the glass became empty (state). 비우다 = to empty/drain it (e.g. 잔을 비우세요 = 'down your glass'). Don't say 잔을 비웠네요 to mean 'it's empty'.
Stating 'your glass is empty' without offering.
In Korean drinking culture it's an implicit offer to refill. Pair it: 잔 비었네요, 한 잔 받으세요 — just noting it and doing nothing can seem inattentive.

usage: Polite; explaining you can't drink much
-는 편이다 softens it to 'tend to be on the weak side'
You can hold your liquor (high tolerance)
The opposite: 세다 ('strong'), said of a strong drinker
examples: 저는 술이 약해서 조금만 마실게요.
I have a low tolerance, so I'll only drink a little.
약해서 ('because weak') gives a polite reason to go slow without fully refusing

A: 한 잔 더 하세요!
B: 저 원래 술이 약해서요. 조금만요.

A: Have one more!
B: I'm naturally a lightweight, so just a little.
A typical 회식 exchange: the offer, and the polite limit-set in response
제가 술이 약한 편이라 한 잔이면 얼굴 빨개져요.
I'm rather a lightweight, so one glass turns my face red.
얼굴(이) 빨개지다 ('face turns red') is a concrete, relatable tell that English speakers can picture
nuance: 술이 약해요 is 술 ('alcohol') + 이 (subject marker) + 약하다 ('to be weak'), meaning 'my alcohol tolerance is weak'. It is the polite, face-saving phrase to announce a low limit before anyone over-pours. The opposite is 술이 세다 (세다 = 'strong'), used for heavy drinkers. The PARTICLE is the classic grammar trap: it must be 술이 약하다 (subject 이), because 약하다 is a descriptive adjective, not a transitive verb — saying 술을 약해요 with the object particle 을 is ungrammatical. The near-synonym 술이 잘 안 받아요 ('alcohol doesn't agree with me') focuses on your body's reaction, while 약하다 focuses on your tolerance level; both are natural. Do not confuse this with 술을 못 마셔요 ('I can't drink at all'): 약하다 means low tolerance — you WILL have some — while 못 마시다 is total inability. Critically, 술이 약해요 is not a hard refusal; in a 회식 it is a polite negotiating move that lets you sip slowly while still participating. Pair it with 조금만 마실게요 ('I'll just have a little') to signal continued social presence.

structuredNuance.t: 술이 약해요 = 'alcohol is weak (for me)'. The literal structure names alcohol as the subject, which feels backwards in English ('I am weak to alcohol'), but the Korean idiom always uses 술이 (subject) not 저는 술에 (topic+to). The real meaning is 'I have a low tolerance' — a polite, social qualifier before someone pours too generously.

Use this early in a 회식 or when being poured for — ideally before the glass is full. With seniors: 저는 술이 약해서 조금만 마실게요 (full polite sentence). With peers/friends: 나 술 약해. This is not a refusal; it signals you'll participate but at a smaller pace.

술이 약해요 (low tolerance, will sip) vs 술을 못 마셔요 (total inability) vs 술이 잘 안 받아요 (doesn't agree with my body, focuses on physical reaction). The dividing line: 약하다 = you'll drink a little; 못 마시다 = you won't drink at all.
Soften with 편이다: 술이 좀 약한 편이에요 ('I tend to be a bit of a lightweight'). Strengthen: 술이 완전 약해요 ('I really can't hold it'). Opposite: 술이 세다 / 술이 강하다 ('high tolerance').

Two traps: (1) the particle — 술을 약해요 is ungrammatical; 약하다 is an adjective needing a subject (이/가), not an object (을/를). (2) Treating this as a hard refusal — it isn't. Saying 술이 약해요 still implies you'll have some; if you cannot drink at all, say 술을 못 마셔요 instead.

mistakes: Saying 술을 약해요 with the object particle.
약하다 is a descriptive adjective; its subject takes 이/가. Correct: 술이 약해요. 술을 약해요 is ungrammatical.
Confusing 술이 약해요 with 술을 못 마셔요.
약하다 = low tolerance (you can drink a little); 못 마시다 = can't drink at all. If you'll still sip, use 술이 약해요, not 못 마셔요.
Translating 'weak to alcohol' as 술에 약해요 by default.
The idiomatic, most natural form is the subject construction 술이 약해요. Lead with that rather than 술에 약해요.

usage: 전혀 ('not at all') + 술(을) 하다 makes it absolute
examples: 죄송한데 저는 술을 못 마셔요. 사이다 마실게요.
Sorry, I can't drink — I'll have cider instead.
Offer a soft alternative (사이다 = lemon-lime soda) to stay social and show you're still participating in the mood
체질상 술을 못 마셔요. 건강상 이유예요.
I can't drink for constitutional reasons — it's a health thing.
체질상 ('due to my constitution/body type') is the gold-standard unarguable reason that shuts down pressure politely

A: 한 잔만 하세요.
B: 저 진짜 술 못 마셔서요. 사이다로 건배할게요!

A: Just have one glass.
B: I really can't drink — I'll toast with cider!
B deflects the push with 못 마시다 + offers a soft-drink toast so the mood doesn't break
nuance: 저는 술 못 마셔요 is 술 ('alcohol') + 못 ('cannot') + 마시다 ('to drink') — stating inability, not choice. The crucial 못 vs. 안 contrast: 못 마셔요 = UNABLE (body, allergy, medication, constitution), while 안 마셔요 = CHOOSING not to (today, or in general). Using 안 to a pushy senior can sound like deliberate refusal ('I won't'), whereas 못 ('I can't') is physiological and harder to argue with, saving both parties' face. 못 마시다 is a total inability — a step beyond 술이 약해요 (low tolerance, will still sip). A particle note: in natural speech 술 못 마셔요 (particle dropped) is common; the fuller 술을 못 마셔요 is also fine. The English-speaker pitfall is expecting one flat 'no' to end pressure. Korean 회식 culture has historically pushed drinks, so reinforce 못 마셔요 with an unarguable reason (운전해야 해서 'I have to drive'; 약 먹고 있어서 'I'm on medication'; 체질상) and offer to toast with a soft drink. A firm 못 마셔요 + reason + cider toast is far more effective than repeating 'no'.

structuredNuance.t: 저는 술 못 마셔요 = 'I cannot drink alcohol (am unable to)'. The word 못 marks inability, not unwillingness. The real social function is not just information but a face-saving exit from the pour cycle — saying 못 마셔요 protects your host too, because they did not cause you discomfort.

저는 술 못 마셔요 is polite-neutral. With seniors add 죄송한데 ('sorry, but') and a reason first. Among friends: 나 술 못 마셔. The firmer formal version: 저는 음주를 못 합니다. Always follow with an alternative drink (사이다, 콜라, 물) to show you'll join the mood.

못 마셔요 (unable — physiological) vs 안 마셔요 (choosing not to — can sound like 'I won't') vs 술이 약해요 (low tolerance, will still sip). With a senior, 못 마셔요 is always safer than 안 마셔요 because inability is unarguable; choice invites persuasion.

Add emphasis: 체질상 술을 전혀 못 마셔요 ('constitutionally cannot drink at all'). Softer variant: 술은 잘 못 해요 ('I'm really not good with alcohol'). Keep the 못 in all forms — never swap to 안 when inability is the point.

The trap is choosing 안 마셔요 when you mean 못 마셔요. 안 = choice (invites 'just one sip!'); 못 = inability (hard to argue with). Also, a bare refusal without a reason or a soft-drink alternative can feel socially abrupt in Korean group settings — always soften with 죄송한데, give a reason, and offer to join with 사이다.

mistakes: Using 안 마셔요 when you mean you physically can't.
안 = choosing not to (can sound like refusing); 못 = unable. To a senior, 못 마셔요 ('I can't') is safer and harder to push back on than 안 마셔요.
Saying just '노' or a bare 'no' to refuse a drink.
A blunt refusal can offend in 회식 culture. Give a reason and an alternative: 술 못 마셔서 사이다 마실게요. Soften the no.
Confusing 못 마셔요 with 안 좋아해요.
안 좋아해요 ('I don't like it') invites persuasion ('just try it!'). 못 마셔요 ('I can't') states inability and ends the negotiation more cleanly.

usage: Polite; asking for a small pour
반 잔 ('half a glass') is a concrete small amount
Said mid-pour to halt the bottle at the current level
examples: 저 술 약해서 조금만 주세요.
I'm a lightweight, so just a little, please.
Lead with the reason (술이 약해서) so the pour-er understands before they fill the glass

A: 얼마나 드릴까요?
B: 조금만요, 거기까지만요!

A: How much should I pour?
B: Just a little — stop right there!
B signals both a small amount and a live stop mid-pour; 거기까지만요 is said DURING the pour
운전해야 해서 반 잔만 받을게요.
I have to drive, so I'll take just half a glass.
운전 ('driving') is an accepted and respected reason to cap intake; 반 잔 gives a concrete, unambiguous amount
nuance: 조금만 주세요 is 조금 ('a little') + 만 ('only') + 주세요 ('please give') — 'only a little, please'. The particle 만 ('only/just') is doing the limiting work; without it, 좀 주세요 is merely a polite request for a pour ('please give', no quantity limit). Many learners say 좀 주세요 thinking it means 'a little' but it actually means 'please give (politely)' — the quantity is unspecified. The most effective live phrase at the table is 거기까지만요 ('just to there'), said mid-pour to stop the bottle at whatever level is in the glass — Koreans use this constantly. For a concrete cap, 반 잔만 주세요 ('just half a glass') leaves nothing ambiguous. The English-speaker pitfall is timing: these words need to come WHILE the person is pouring, not after. Staying silent until the glass is full and then complaining is the non-native move. Gesture matters too: you can slightly bow or tilt the glass toward the pourer to signal 'good, stop'. Abruptly covering the glass with your hand toward a senior can feel rude; a verbal 조금만 주세요 with a slight bow is the graceful version.

structuredNuance.t: 조금만 주세요 = 'give (me) only a little'. The word 만 ('only') is the quantity limiter, not the politeness marker 좀. Without 만 — 좀 주세요 — you get 'please pour (politely)' with no amount limit. That single particle 만 is what makes this a request for less, not just a polite request.

Say this as the bottle tilts toward your glass, not after. Polite with seniors: 조금만 주세요 or 거기까지만요 with a slight bow. Casual with friends: 조금만 줘 or 거기서 멈춰. The mid-pour stop phrase 거기까지만요 is essential regardless of register.

조금만 주세요 (small amount, polite) vs 반 잔만 주세요 (half a glass, more specific) vs 거기까지만요 (live stop mid-pour, very practical) vs 됐어요 ('that's enough / no more', used after a full-glass pour). 됐어요 declines further; 조금만 shapes the current pour.
Scale the limit: 조금만 (a little) → 반 잔만 (half a glass) → 한 모금만 (just a sip). Live stop: 거기까지만요 / 거기면 충분해요. Accept but limit: 딱 조금만 주세요 (딱 = exactly, reinforces the cap).

Three traps: (1) saying 좀 주세요 thinking it means 'a little' — it doesn't; add 만 for quantity. (2) Saying it AFTER the glass is full — speak up MID-pour. (3) Slapping a hand over the glass toward a senior — use words and a slight tilt of the glass instead.

mistakes: Saying 좀 주세요 to mean 'a little'.
좀 is a politeness softener, not a quantity; it means 'please give'. For a small amount use 조금만 주세요 (만 = 'only/just').
Staying silent during the pour, then saying it's too much.
Speak up mid-pour: 조금만요 or 거기까지만요 ('just to there'). Korean pouring is interactive; you signal the amount as it's poured.
Covering the glass with your hand toward a senior.
Abruptly capping a senior's pour can read as rude. Instead say 조금만 주세요 and tilt the glass slightly; a verbal limit is more polite.

usage: Polite; the buzz/drunkenness has worn off
I need to sober up a bit
-아야겠다 = 'I'd better ~'; you intend to sober up
I can't shake the alcohol / still drunk
안 깨다 = it won't wear off (e.g. next morning)
examples: 바람 좀 쐬니까 술 깼어요.
Getting some fresh air sobered me up.
바람(을) 쐬다 ('get some air outside') is the standard first step to sober up — the go-to before deciding to drive

A: 아직 좀 취한 것 같아요.
B: 해장국 먹으면 술이 좀 깰 거예요.

A: I think I'm still a bit drunk.
B: Hangover soup will help you sober up.
해장국 (haejang-guk) is the classic next-day remedy; B reassures A with practical advice
아직 술이 안 깬 것 같아요. 운전 안 할게요.
I don't think I'm sober yet — I won't drive.
안 깬 것 같다 ('seems not sober yet') is the responsible self-assessment before DUI risk; the sentence models good judgment
nuance: 술 깨다 is 술 ('alcohol') + 깨다 ('to wake from / break out of a state') — to come out of drunkenness, i.e. 'sober up'. The PARTICLE trap: 깨다 is intransitive here — the state changes on its own — so it is 술이 깨다 / 술(이) 깼어요, NOT 술을 깨다 (술을 would make 깨다 transitive, which is wrong here; 술을 깨다 is not a natural form). To express deliberate effort, use purpose framing: 술 좀 깨야겠어요 ('I'd better sober up') or 술 깨려고 바람 쐬러 나갔어요 ('went out for air to sober up'). Watch 깨다's homographs: it also means 'to break (a dish)' and 'to hatch (an egg)' — context with 술 fixes the 'sober up' meaning. Don't confuse with 깨우다 (transitive 'wake someone up'): 술 깼어요 = I sobered up (happens to me); 깨우다 = you wake another person. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 정신 차리다 ('snap out of it / regain focus') — that phrase is about mental alertness, not metabolizing alcohol; for the physical wearing-off of a buzz, use 술 깨다. Key collocations: 술이 깼다 (sobered), 술이 안 깬다 (still drunk), 술 깨는 데 좋다 ('good for sobering up', said of 해장국/꿀물).

structuredNuance.t: 술 깼어요 = 'the alcohol has broken/woken' (intransitive). The literal image is the drunken state cracking open and passing. In real use it means 'I've sobered up' — the buzz is gone, the alcohol has metabolized. It does NOT mean you woke up (일어났어요) or snapped to attention (정신 차렸어요).

Use this to report your state: 술 깼어요 (I'm sober now). To say you plan to sober up: 술 좀 깨야겠어요. To describe still being drunk: 술이 안 깨요. Register: 깼어요 (polite), 깼어 (casual). Comes up before deciding to drive, call a 대리운전, or before a next-day commitment.

술 깨다 (sober up, intransitive, alcohol wears off) vs 정신 차리다 (regain focus/alertness, NOT about alcohol) vs 깨우다 (transitive, wake someone else up). The alcohol-sobriety meaning is uniquely 깨다 with 술 as subject or dropped-particle companion.
State: 술이 깼어요 / 술 깼어요. Still drunk: 술이 안 깨요. Intention: 술 좀 깨야겠어요 / 깨려고요. Cause: -면 깰 거예요 ('if X, you'll sober up').

Two traps: (1) 술을 깼어요 with the object particle — wrong; 깨다 here is intransitive, so the subject particle (이/가) or no particle is correct. (2) Using 정신 차렸어요 to mean 'I sobered up' — that phrase is about alertness/composure, not blood-alcohol. Always use 술 깼어요 for the physical sobriety.

mistakes: Saying 술을 깼어요 with the object particle.
깨다 ('to sober up') is intransitive; the alcohol/state is the subject: 술이 깼어요. 술을 깼어요 is wrong.
Using 정신 차리다 to mean 'sober up'.
정신(을) 차리다 means 'snap out of it / get focused', about alertness. For the alcohol physically wearing off, use 술(이) 깨다.
Confusing 깨다 (sober up) with 깨우다 (wake someone).
술 깼어요 = I sobered up (happened to me). 깨우다 is transitive 'to wake another person'. Don't say 술 깨웠어요 for yourself sobering up.

english: What snacks should we order (to go with drinks)?
usage: Polite; proposing to pick drinking food for the table
What should we get to snack on?
Asking the staff for a popular drinking dish
Does it come with a basic snack?
기본 안주 = the free starter snack some bars give automatically
examples: 술만 마시면 속 버려요. 안주 뭐 시킬까요?
Drinking on an empty stomach is rough — what anju should we order?
속(을) 버리다 ('ruin your stomach') explains WHY 안주 is not optional; ordering without 안주 is called 깡술
여기 안주 뭐가 맛있어요?
What anju is good here?
Simple question to staff; the phrasing 뭐가 맛있어요 ('what is tasty') invites a personal recommendation

A: 치킨에 맥주, 이게 진리죠. 치맥으로 시킬까요?
B: 완전 찬성!

A: Chicken with beer — that's the truth. Shall we order 치맥?
B: Totally agree!
치맥 (치킨+맥주) is Korea's most iconic 안주+술 pair; 진리 ('the truth') is playful hyperbole for a perfect combo
nuance: 안주 is food eaten specifically WITH alcohol — there is no clean English equivalent. Do not translate it as 반찬 (small dishes that accompany a rice meal) or as 간식 (a between-meals snack anytime); 안주 exists only in the drinking context: 골뱅이무침, 두부김치, 치킨, or 마른안주 (dried bar snacks). 뭐 시킬까요? uses the 'shall we?' ending -ㄹ까요? to float a suggestion to the group rather than commanding — the polite, inclusive way to open a decision. 시키다 ('to order food/service') is the natural everyday choice here; 주문하다 is also fine but feels a notch more formal. The cultural note that changes how this phrase lands: drinking 'dry' — no 안주 at all — is called 깡술 and is generally frowned upon. Proposing 안주 뭐 시킬까요? early is the socially smooth move that says 'let's do this properly'. Classic 안주 pairings to know: 치맥 (치킨+맥주), 소맥 (소주+맥주 mix), 삼겹살+소주, 마른안주+막걸리. The English-speaker pitfall is the 반찬 vs 안주 confusion — calling the bar's drinking dishes 반찬 sounds like mixing up restaurant categories, and asking for free 반찬 at a 호프집 (beer pub) confuses the staff.

structuredNuance.t: 안주 뭐 시킬까요? = 'What anju shall we order?' The word 안주 has no English equivalent: it is food eaten specifically to accompany alcohol, not a side dish with a meal (반찬) and not an any-time snack (간식). Using either substitute makes you sound like you don't know the drinking context.

Say this as soon as drinks are ordered — before glasses are poured, ideally. It signals you know the culture (no 깡술). At a 회식 the junior often takes the initiative to ask. With peers: 안주 뭐 시킬까? Asking staff: 여기 뭐가 맛있어요? / 추천 안주 있어요?

안주 (food WITH alcohol) vs 반찬 (side dishes WITH rice) vs 간식 (anytime snack). All three are 'food alongside something', but the companion defines the word. Also: 시키다 ('order food/service') vs 주문하다 ('place an order', more formal). 시킬까요? is the natural table-talk verb.
Change the verb: 뭐 먹을까요? ('what shall we eat?') is also fine but less specific. Add specifics: 치킨 시킬까요? (direct), 마른안주만 시킬까요? (just dried snacks). Ask staff: 안주 추천해 주세요.

Two traps: (1) calling 안주 반찬 or 간식 — these are wrong-register words in a bar context; always use 안주 at a drinking table. (2) Skipping 안주 altogether: drinking without it is 깡술, considered bad form — proposing to order 안주 is not optional, it is the expected social move.

mistakes: Calling drinking food 반찬 instead of 안주.
반찬 = side dishes with a rice meal; 안주 = food eaten with alcohol. At a bar, order 안주, not 반찬.
Translating 안주 as 'snack' (간식).
간식 is a between-meals snack anytime. 안주 specifically accompanies drinking. They're not interchangeable.
Using a command instead of -ㄹ까요? to suggest.
안주 시켜요 sounds like telling people to order. 안주 뭐 시킬까요? ('shall we order?') invites the group to decide together.

english: Would it be okay if I head out first?
usage: Polite; asking the senior's leave to go early
Apologetic softener when slipping out early
examples: 부장님, 내일 일찍 출근해야 해서 저 먼저 일어나도 될까요?
Director, I have an early start tomorrow — may I head out first?
Give the reason (내일 일찍 출근) BEFORE the request; reasons first is the Korean social order for asking permission

A: 죄송한데 막차 시간이라 먼저 일어나 보겠습니다.
B: 그래요, 조심해서 가요.

A: I'm sorry, but it's last-train time, so I'll head out first.
B: Okay, get home safe.
막차 ('last train/bus') is an accepted, respected reason; B's response shows a senior releasing the junior graciously
먼저 일어나서 죄송합니다. 잘 먹었습니다. 내일 뵙겠습니다.
Sorry to leave first. The food was wonderful. See you tomorrow.
The three-line exit formula: apology + gratitude for the meal + see-you — never skip any of these at a 회식
nuance: 저 먼저 일어나도 될까요? is 저 ('I', humble) + 먼저 ('first/before others') + 일어나다 ('to get up/rise') + -아도 되다 ('may I ~') + -ㄹ까요? ('would it be...?'). The key idiom is 일어나다 — literally 'to stand up', but the polite euphemism for LEAVING a gathering. Koreans avoid saying 가다 ('go') bluntly to a senior when leaving; 일어나다 or 들어가다 ('go in/home') softens the departure. The -아도 될까요? frame asks permission, which matters because leaving before the most senior person at a 회식 is socially sensitive — you must signal, give a reason, and ask leave rather than just standing up. Contrast 먼저 일어날게요 ('I'll head out first', softer announcement to peers) with 먼저 일어나도 될까요? (asking permission, for seniors). The English-speaker pitfall is using 떠날게요 — 떠나다 means 'depart' in the journey/relationship sense and sounds dramatic for leaving dinner — or bluntly saying 갈게요 to the boss, which can feel abrupt. Also, vanishing silently is rude: Korean etiquette requires you to address the senior, apologize lightly, thank them for the meal, and formally bid goodbye. The clean exit formula: 잘 먹었습니다, 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다.

structuredNuance.t: 저 먼저 일어나도 될까요? = 'May it be okay if I get up/rise first?' The word 일어나다 ('to stand up') is a euphemism for leaving — you do not literally just stand; you are requesting permission to end your participation in the gathering. The literal 'I'm going' (갈게요) is considered too blunt.

Use this when leaving a 회식 or group gathering before the senior does. Signal it early (before the taxi app is open). Polite-permission form (-아도 될까요?) with seniors. Peer announcement: 나 먼저 갈게. Formal deferential: 저 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다. Always give a reason first.

먼저 일어나도 될까요? (permission-asking, for seniors) vs 먼저 일어날게요 (softer announcement, for peers) vs 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다 (most formal, 'I'll be heading in now') vs 먼저 갈게 (casual, friends only). Never use 떠날게요 ('I'll depart') for a dinner exit — it sounds like leaving a city.
The -아도 되다 permission structure: 일어나도 돼요? (친구), 일어나도 될까요? (polite), 일어나도 되겠습니까? (very formal). Add apology: 죄송하지만 먼저 일어나도 될까요? Full exit sequence: 잘 먹었습니다 → 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다 → 내일 뵙겠습니다.

Three traps: (1) using 떠날게요 — 떠나다 is for journeys or partings, not dinner exits; (2) saying 갈게요 ('I'll go') bluntly to a boss — too flat; (3) slipping out without speaking — silent exits are rude at 회식. Always address, apologize, thank, and bid farewell.

mistakes: Saying 떠날게요 to mean 'I'll leave (the dinner)'.
떠나다 = depart (a place for good, a trip). For leaving a gathering, use 일어나다 or 들어가다: 먼저 일어날게요 / 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다.
Bluntly saying 저 갈게요 to a senior.
갈게요 ('I'll go') is flat and can seem abrupt to a boss. The polite euphemism is 먼저 일어나도 될까요? or 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다.
Leaving without telling the senior.
Slipping out silently is rude in 회식 culture. Signal early, give a reason, and ask leave: 먼저 일어나도 될까요?

usage: Polite; signaling you'll pace yourself without refusing
Take it easy / don't overdo it
Said to someone who's drinking too much; can also mean 'cut it out'
Let's drink in moderation and head home
Wrapping the night sensibly; 들어가다 = go home
examples: 내일 회의 있어서 오늘은 적당히 마실게요.
I have a meeting tomorrow, so I'll go easy today.
A reason (내일 회의) makes pacing yourself acceptable in 회식 culture; announcing it early heads off 원샷 pressure
자자, 다들 적당히 마셔요. 무리하지 말고.
Come on, everyone pace yourselves — don't overdo it.
무리하지 말다 ('don't push it') reinforces moderation; a senior saying this gives everyone cover to slow down

A: 한 잔 더 하세요!
B: 저는 오늘 적당히만 할게요. 내일 운전해야 해서요.

A: Have one more!
B: I'll just keep it moderate today — I have to drive tomorrow.
B uses 적당히만 할게요 + a reason to decline more without flat-out refusing — the socially graceful 회식 move
nuance: 적당히 is the adverb of 적당하다 ('to be appropriate/moderate', Sino-Korean 適當), so 적당히 마시다 = 'drink an appropriate amount' — pace yourself, don't get hammered. It is the graceful way to set a personal limit without refusing outright, because it acknowledges you will drink, just not excessively. Register nuance: 적당히 마실게요 (about yourself, your own limit) vs 적당히 하세요 / 드세요 (telling someone ELSE to slow down, which can feel mildly scolding — don't aim this at the boss). Note that 적당히 해! in non-drinking contexts means 'knock it off!', so tone and topic matter. The near-synonym 알아서 마실게요 ('I'll drink as I see fit') overlaps but can sound slightly dismissive; 적당히 is softer and warmer. The English-speaker pitfall is the translation: 'moderately' tempts learners to say 보통으로 ('normally/usually') or 중간으로 ('in the middle'), neither of which fits drinking amounts — the idiomatic adverb is 적당히. Grammatically, 적당히 is an adverb modifying 마시다 — don't use the noun stem alone (적당 마시다 is wrong; you need the -히 adverb form). Culturally, saying this early at a 회식 heads off the 원샷 pressure cycle before it starts.

structuredNuance.t: 적당히 = 'to an appropriate degree'. 적당히 마실게요 = 'I will drink to an appropriate/fitting degree'. The real meaning is 'I'll pace myself' — you are NOT refusing to drink, you are capping the amount. That subtlety makes it socially useful: it participates without over-committing.

Say this about yourself early in the drinking session, especially before 원샷 pressure builds. 적당히 마실게요 is about your own limit (polite). 적당히 드세요 / 하세요 targets someone else — use carefully; with a boss, soften to 천천히 드세요 ('please take your time') instead. 적당히 마시자 among friends is relaxed and friendly.

적당히 마실게요 (set my own moderate limit) vs 조금만 마실게요 ('I'll only have a little', smaller actual amount) vs 천천히 마실게요 ('I'll drink slowly', about pace not volume) vs 알아서 할게요 ('I'll handle it myself', slightly dismissive). 적당히 is the warmest and most socially flexible.
적당히 is the adverb of 적당하다, Sino-Korean 適當 (適 = fit/appropriate, 當 = proper/right). The -히 ending is the standard adjective-to-adverb marker in Korean.

Three traps: (1) using 보통으로 ('normally') or 중간으로 ('in the middle') — neither works for drinking amount; use 적당히. (2) dropping -히 and saying 적당 마시다 — wrong; 적당히 is required as an adverb. (3) using 적당히 하세요 toward a boss — it can sound like 'cut it out', mildly scolding; use 천천히 드세요 instead.

mistakes: Saying 보통으로 마실게요 for 'moderately'.
보통으로 means 'normally/usually', not 'a moderate amount'. The right adverb for pacing your drinking is 적당히: 적당히 마실게요.
Dropping the -히: 적당 마시다.
적당 is the noun stem; you need the adverb 적당히 to modify 마시다. Say 적당히 마실게요, not 적당 마셔요.
Using 적당히 하세요 lightly to a senior.
적당히 해/하세요 can sound like 'cut it out', mildly scolding. Toward a boss, soften to 천천히 드세요 ('please pace yourself') or 무리하지 마세요.

english: Shall we go to the second round (next venue)?
usage: Shall we go for a second round?
Polite; proposing to move to the next place
Where shall we go for round two?
Asking where the next venue should be
I'll sit out the second round
빠지다 ('to drop out') = the graceful way to skip the next round
examples: 1차 끝났으니까 2차 갈까요?
Round one's done — shall we go for round two?
1차 끝나다 ('the first round is over') is the natural cue to propose 2차; -ㄹ까요? floats it as a group decision

A: 2차로 노래방 어때요?
B: 좋죠! 근처에 있는 데 가요.

A: How about karaoke for round two?
B: Sounds great! Let's go somewhere nearby.
노래방 (karaoke room) is the classic 2차 choice; B's 좋죠 ('isn't it great!') signals enthusiastic agreement
저는 내일 일찍 일어나야 해서 2차는 빠질게요. 오늘 정말 즐거웠어요!
I have to get up early, so I'll skip round two. Tonight was really fun!
빠질게요 + a warm closing remark lets you leave after 1차 without dampening the mood for the rest of the group
nuance: 2차 (이차, Sino-Korean 二次, 'second time/round') means the NEXT VENUE after the first — Korean nights out famously go 1차 (dinner + drinks) → 2차 (another bar, or 노래방 karaoke) → sometimes 3차, 4차. The 차 counter takes Sino-Korean numbers (일차, 이차, 삼차), unlike most counters — '이차' NOT '두 차'. 2차 갈까요? uses -ㄹ까요? to float the suggestion to the group. The key paired phrase is 빠지다 ('drop out'): 2차는 빠질게요 is the graceful way to leave after the first round — far more natural than refusing the whole evening or making a scene. The English-speaker pitfall is conceptual: 'second round' in English sounds like another round of the SAME drinks at the SAME table, but Korean 2차 means physically RELOCATING to a new venue — do not say 2차 if you just want another bottle where you are; use 한 잔 더 for that. Culturally, 2차 attendance can feel semi-obligatory in a company 회식 depending on the workplace culture; juniors often need a clear reason (막차, early meeting) to bow out, so 2차는 빠질게요 + a warm reason is the socially smooth exit.

structuredNuance.t: 2차 갈까요? = 'Shall we go to the second round?' The literal 차 means 'time/round', and 2차 specifically means RELOCATING to a new venue for the second leg of the night — NOT another round of drinks at the same table. That relocation is the key difference from the English 'second round'.

Propose 2차 갈까요? as the bill for 1차 is being settled or the group is naturally winding down the first venue. Polite -ㄹ까요? is safe for any group. To bow out: 2차는 빠질게요 + a reason. Junior bowing out of 회식 2차: always give a reason (막차, 내일 일찍, 운전) or you may seem unsociable.

2차 갈까요? (propose next venue) vs 한 잔 더 할까요? (another drink at the same place) vs 오늘은 여기서 끝내죠 (let's call it here). The 1차/2차/3차 system describes a complete night-out structure with physical moves between venues, not just successive orders of drinks.
2차 (이차) is Sino-Korean 二次, 'second time/round'. The 차 counter takes Sino-Korean numbers (일차, 이차, 삼차), unlike most counters which take native Korean numbers. 두 차 is wrong.

Two traps: (1) thinking '2차' means more drinks at the same spot — it means a NEW venue; (2) using native numbers: 두 차 is wrong; the counter is Sino-Korean: 이차 (2차), 삼차 (3차). Also, bowing out of 2차 at a company 회식 requires a polite reason; a bare 빠질게요 without explanation can seem rude depending on the workplace.

mistakes: Thinking 2차 means 'another round of drinks' at the same table.
2차 means moving to a NEW venue (another bar, karaoke). For just more drinks where you are, say 한 잔 더 (one more glass), not 2차.
Saying 두 차 with a native number.
The round counter 차 takes Sino-Korean numbers: 일차, 이차, 삼차. 'Second round' is 이차(2차), not 두 차.
Refusing the whole night instead of just 2차.
You can stay for 1차 and bow out gracefully: 2차는 빠질게요 (빠지다 = drop out). No need to decline the entire 회식.

english: Let's cut down the number of rounds
usage: Let's go easy on the rounds
Polite-suggestive; -시죠 proposes to a senior gently without commanding
Let's do just round one today
Concrete cap: end the night after the first venue
슬슬 마무리하다 ('gradually wind down'); 슬슬 softens the suggestion
Let's do it properly next time
Defers the big night to another day; politely saves face for everyone
examples: 내일 다들 출근하는데 오늘은 차수 좀 줄이시죠.
Everyone works tomorrow, so let's cut the rounds short today.
A shared reason (내일 출근) makes the suggestion feel caring rather than limiting; the junior nudges the boss without confronting
1차에서 깔끔하게 끝내고 들어가시죠.
Let's wrap up cleanly after round one and head home.
깔끔하게 끝내다 ('end it cleanly/neatly') frames going home as the refined, sensible choice rather than a party-pooper move

A: 3차까지 가야죠!
B: 요즘 회식 문화도 바뀌어서 오늘은 차수 좀 줄이시죠.

A: We have to go to round three!
B: Drinking culture has changed lately, so let's cut it short today.
B uses a cultural shift argument to deflect — impersonal and face-saving for everyone at the table
nuance: 차수(를) 줄이다 is 차수 ('number of rounds', 次數) + 줄이다 ('to reduce') — cut down how many 차 (1차/2차/3차) the night runs. The ending -시죠 (honorific 시 + suggestive 죠 = 지요) proposes an action to a SENIOR softly and deferentially, like 'shall we...?', 'why don't we...?' — a junior can nudge the boss toward going home without sounding bossy or confrontational. This is far more face-preserving than the plain 줄여요 or a direct command. Compare the three near-synonyms: 줄이다 ('reduce the count of rounds') vs 끝내다 ('end it entirely') vs 마무리하다 ('wrap up / bring to a close'); 차수 줄이시죠 trims the rounds while 마무리하죠 proposes ending altogether. 차수 is fairly advanced drinking vocabulary — many learners know 1차/2차 but not the umbrella noun 차수, so using it signals real fluency. Culturally, this phrase is most valuable when the night has gone to 3차 or later and you can see people flagging: framing it as a shared sensible decision (내일 출근, 막차) rather than a personal complaint is the smooth move. Companion phrases: 슬슬 일어나시죠 ('shall we get going?'), 오늘은 여기까지 하시죠 ('let's call it here').

structuredNuance.t: 차수 좀 줄이시죠 = 'shall we reduce the number of rounds a bit?' 차수 is the total count of rounds (1차, 2차, 3차…); 줄이다 = reduce it. The real meaning is 'let's not drag this into 3차/4차' — a tactful cap on the night's length, not a refusal to drink.

Use this when the night has run past the expected end or people look tired/drunk. The -시죠 ending is key: it makes the suggestion deferential to a senior (junior → boss is the typical direction). Among peers: 오늘은 2차까지만 하자. Direct command to the boss (줄여요) is too flat; -시죠 softens it into an invitation.

차수 줄이시죠 (reduce the round-count, keep the night shorter) vs 마무리하시죠 (wrap up entirely, go home now) vs 2차는 빠질게요 (I personally will skip). 줄이다 is a trim; 마무리하다 is an ending. Use 줄이다 when you can tolerate one more round but not three.
차수 is Sino-Korean 次數 (次 = time/round, 數 = number/count) — the umbrella noun over the individual 차 (1차/2차/3차). Knowing 차수 as a word marks intermediate-advanced fluency.

Two traps: (1) using plain 줄여요 or a command to a boss — too blunt, sounds like you're ordering; always use -시죠 for a deferential suggestion; (2) saying 그만 마셔요 ('stop drinking') directly to a senior — face-threatening and presumptuous. Use 차수 줄이시죠 + a shared reason instead.

mistakes: Telling a senior 그만 마셔요 ('stop drinking').
That's blunt and face-threatening to a boss. Suggest softly with -시죠 and a reason: 오늘은 차수 좀 줄이시죠 / 슬슬 마무리하시죠.
Confusing 차수 (number of rounds) with 차 (a single round).
차 is one leg (1차, 2차); 차수 is the count of rounds overall. 차수를 줄이다 = reduce the total number of rounds.
Using plain 줄여요 to the boss.
줄여요 is flat. The deferential suggestion form is -시죠: 차수 좀 줄이시죠, which proposes it respectfully to a senior.

english: I'll sober up a bit before I go
usage: I'll sober up a bit then go
I'll sober up then head out
I'll step out for some air
바람(을) 쐬다 = the standard sobering move; 올게요 ('I'll come back') suggests you'll return
I'll sober up over a coffee
Getting caffeine to clear your head before deciding to drive or go home
examples: 운전해야 해서 저 술 좀 깨고 갈게요.
I have to drive, so I'll sober up a bit first.
운전 ('driving') is the responsible reason and the most common real-life trigger for this phrase — tied to Korea's strict DUI laws

A: 지금 바로 가요?
B: 아니요, 속이 좀 안 좋아서 바람 쐬고 술 좀 깨고 갈게요.

A: Are you leaving right now?
B: No, I feel a bit off — I'll get some air and sober up first.
B chains two steps: 바람 쐬고 ('get air') then 술 깨고 ('sober up') — the realistic sequence before a safe exit
대리 부르기 전에 술 좀 깨려고요.
I'm trying to sober up before calling a designated driver.
대리(운전) = a paid proxy driver who drives your car home — the responsible Korean DUI alternative; 깨려고요 = the intent to sober up
nuance: 저 술 좀 깨고 갈게요 chains 술 깨다 ('sober up') + -고 ('and then') + 가다 ('go'), with 좀 softening the whole: 'I'll sober up a little and THEN go.' The sequential connector -고 is the grammar lesson: it orders the actions sober-up THEN leave, signaling you are not leaving immediately. Even in casual speech the particle 이 is often dropped, so 술 깨고 갈게요 (without 이) is perfectly natural. This phrase is the responsible-adult move tied to Korea's strict 음주운전 (drunk driving) laws: options are 술 깨고 가다 (wait it out), 대리운전 (paid proxy driver), 택시, or 지하철. Don't 직역 'sleep it off' as 자고 갈게요 unless you literally plan to sleep there — the sobriety-waiting meaning is 술 좀 깨고 갈게요. Also avoid 정신 차리고 갈게요 for this; 정신 차리다 is about regaining focus, not metabolizing alcohol. Folk sobering remedies to recognize: 바람 쐬다 (get fresh air), 꿀물 (honey water), 헛개차 (hovenia tea). Saying this signals both responsibility and maturity — and often prompts someone to offer coffee, water, or a snack.

structuredNuance.t: 저 술 좀 깨고 갈게요 = 'I will sober up a little and then go'. The -고 connector specifies the ORDER (sober first, then leave), telling listeners you are staying a bit longer. The real meaning is 'don't worry, I'm being responsible — I'll wait until I'm safe to leave'.

Use this when you've had too much to drive or feel unsteady. Polite: 술 좀 깨고 갈게요. Casual (friends): 나 술 좀 깨고 갈게. Express intent to sober: 술 깨야겠어요 ('I need to sober up'). Often follows a statement of how much you drank: 많이 마셨으니까 술 좀 깨고 갈게요.

술 깨고 갈게요 (wait here to sober, then leave) vs 바람 쐬고 올게요 (step outside briefly, implies returning) vs 대리 불러야겠어요 (need to call a proxy driver — not waiting, just not driving yourself). The -고 갈게요 means you are staying; -고 올게요 means stepping out briefly.

Sequence: 술 깨고 갈게요 (then leave) / 술 깨고 올게요 (step out and come back). Intent: 술 좀 깨야겠어요 ('I should sober up'). Cause: 술 깨려고 바람 쐬러 나갔어요 ('went out for air to sober up'). Ongoing: 술이 안 깨요 ('still not sober').

Three traps: (1) 술을 깨고 갈게요 with the object particle — 깨다 is intransitive here, so drop 을 or use 이: 술이 깨고/술 깨고; (2) 직역 'sleep it off' as 자고 갈게요 — that means 'I'll sleep (here) then go'; (3) 정신 차리고 갈게요 — that means 'regain my composure then leave', not 'sober up'.

mistakes: Saying 술을 깨고 갈게요 with the object particle.
깨다 (sober up) is intransitive: 술이 깨다. Say 술 깨고 갈게요 (particle often dropped in speech), not 술을 깨고.
Translating 'sleep it off' literally as 자고 갈게요.
That just means 'I'll sleep (here) then go'. To mean sobering up, say 술 좀 깨고 갈게요. Only use 자다 if you actually plan to sleep.
Using 정신 차리고 갈게요 for sobering up.
정신 차리다 = regain focus/composure, not metabolize alcohol. For the buzz wearing off, use 술 깨고 갈게요.

usage: Polite-casual; offering to pay for everyone's bill
한턱내다 ('treat to a feast'); warmer/idiomatic, implies a notable occasion
살게요 ('I'll buy'); offering to reciprocate at the next gathering
examples: 승진했으니까 오늘은 제가 쏠게요!
I got promoted, so today's on me!
A milestone (승진 = promotion) is the classic reason to treat; the group expects it and the payer earns social points
오늘 제가 살 테니까 마음껏 드세요.
It's on me today, so eat and drink all you want.
마음껏 드세요 ('please help yourself freely') is the natural follow-up; it liberates the guests to order without hesitation

A: 오늘은 제가 쏠게요!
B: 에이, 그럼 다음엔 제가 살게요.

A: Today's on me!
B: Come on, then I'll get it next time.
The reciprocal payment culture: B doesn't argue but commits to paying next time — the graceful Korean counter-offer
nuance: 쏘다 literally means 'to shoot', but in casual Korean slang 쏘다 = 'to treat / foot the entire bill'. 제가 쏠게요 = 'I will shoot (pay) for everyone.' It is upbeat and casual — great with coworkers or friends, but a bit informal for a very stiff or highly formal setting, where 제가 사겠습니다 (사다 'buy') or 제가 한턱내겠습니다 sound more proper. Three near-synonyms: 사다 (neutral 'buy' — 제가 살게요), 쏘다 (breezy slang 'treat'), and 한턱내다 ('treat to a feast', warm and idiomatic, implies a generous spread for a celebration). The English-speaker pitfall is the 직역 trap: 'it's on me' has no Korean equivalent with 'on + me/위에'; you MUST use 쏘다/사다/내다. Also note Korean paying culture: people often genuinely fight over the bill (서로 내려고 한다), the senior typically treats juniors, and 더치페이 (splitting evenly) is less default than in the West. So offering 제가 쏠게요 is a real social gesture that earns warmth, and a graceful reply when someone else insists on paying is 그럼 다음엔 제가 살게요 ('then I'll get it next time'). Conjugation note: 쏘다 is a regular vowel-stem verb — the future -ㄹ게요 attaches to 쏘- → 쏠게요; cf. 사다 → 살게요, 내다 → 낼게요.

structuredNuance.t: 쏘다 = 'to shoot'. 제가 쏠게요 literally means 'I will shoot', but the slang meaning is 'I will foot the entire bill for everyone'. There is NO Korean phrase mirroring 'it's on me' word-for-word — you must use the verb: 쏘다, 사다, or 내다.

쏠게요 is warm and casual — use it with friends, coworkers, or in a group where you know everyone. Toward seniors or in formal settings, upgrade to 제가 사겠습니다 or 한턱내겠습니다. Typical occasions: promotion (승진), birthday (생일), passing an exam (합격), paycheck (월급날).

쏘다 (breezy slang, most casual) vs 사다 (neutral, 'buy') vs 내다 ('put out', neutral) vs 한턱내다 ('treat to a feast', warmest, implies celebration). All mean treating, but 한턱내다 implies the most generosity and is usually tied to a specific good-news occasion.
쏘다 → 쏠게요 (future polite), 쐈어요 (past, 'I treated'), 쏴! (casual command, 'treat us!'). 사다 → 살게요 / 샀어요. 내다 → 낼게요 / 냈어요. 한턱내다 → 한턱낼게요 / 한턱냈어요.
Two traps: (1) direct-translating 'it's on me' — there is no 위에 idiom in Korean; use 쏘다/사다/내다; (2) using 쏘다 in a formal context with a boss — it's too casual; upgrade to 제가 사겠습니다 or 한턱내겠습니다.

mistakes: Translating 'it's on me' word-for-word.
There's no '~위에 있다' idiom for treating in Korean. Use 제가 쏠게요 / 제가 살게요 / 제가 낼게요 instead.
Using slang 쏘다 in a very formal setting.
쏘다 is breezy. To a senior or in a stiff context, prefer 제가 사겠습니다 or 제가 한턱내겠습니다, which sound more proper.
Confusing 한턱내다 with 한 턱 (one chin/jaw).
한턱내다 is a set idiom 'to treat to a meal', not literally a 'jaw'. Use it whole: 제가 한턱낼게요.

usage: Polite; reassuring you're still fine — though often unconvincing
반말, with friends — the classic protest
I think I'm a little tipsy
Honestly admitting a buzz; -ㄴ 것 같다 softens to 'I think / it seems'
Said to someone else who's clearly had too much
examples: 저 진짜 안 취했어요. 한 잔 더 할 수 있어요.
I'm really not drunk — I can have one more.
진짜 ('really/truly') adds insistence; this is the classic protest that often backfires by inviting another pour
살짝 취한 것 같긴 한데 괜찮아요. 물 마실게요.
I might be slightly tipsy, but I'm okay — I'll have some water.
살짝 ('slightly') + 것 같다 is the honest, face-saving middle-ground; pivoting to 물 ('water') is the smart follow-up

A: 많이 취하신 것 같아요. 물 한 잔 드세요.
B: 아, 안 취했어요. 괜찮아요!

A: You seem quite drunk — have a glass of water.
B: Oh, I'm not drunk! I'm fine!
A's concern vs B's (unconvincing) protest — the archetypal 회식 exchange
nuance: 취하다 ('to get drunk/intoxicated') is the core verb; 안 취했어요 = 'I'm not drunk', literally 'I didn't get drunk'. The TENSE TRAP is crucial: Korean uses the PAST 취했어요 to describe the CURRENT state of being drunk — the getting-drunk happened, so you are now IN that resulting state. This is the same change-of-state pattern as 잘생겼어요 ('is good-looking') or 문이 열렸어요 ('the door is open'): past form names the present condition. So 'I am drunk' = 취했어요, NOT 취해요; 'I'm not drunk' = 안 취했어요, NOT 안 취해요. Degrees of intoxication: 살짝/조금 취하다 (tipsy), 많이 취하다 (very drunk), 만취하다 (blackout/dead drunk, 滿醉 'full-drunk'), 꽐라(가) 되다 (slangy for wasted). A cultural trap: blurting 안 취했어요 loudly at a 회식 is paradoxically a sign people suspect you ARE drunk — the person insisting hardest is usually the most intoxicated. If you genuinely want to stop drinking, admitting 조금 취한 것 같아요 and asking for water is more effective. Companion expression: 술기운(이) 오르다 ('the alcohol is hitting me'). 취하다 has an unrelated homonym ('take/adopt a measure' — 조치를 취하다), but context with 술 disambiguates completely.

structuredNuance.t: 안 취했어요 = 'I didn't get drunk (and so am not now in that state)'. The past form 취했어요 is the CURRENT drunk state (change-of-state pattern). The real social meaning of 안 취했어요, 괜찮아요 is a protest/reassurance that is often self-undermining — the louder the protest, the less convincing it usually is.

Use 안 취했어요 or 조금 취한 것 같아요 depending on how honest you want to be. To someone genuinely concerned: 살짝 취한 것 같긴 한데 괜찮아요 + 물 마실게요 is more convincing than denial. To assess someone else: 많이 취하신 것 같아요, 물 드세요 (polite concern).
안 취했어요 (denial — I'm not drunk) vs 조금 취했어요 (admission — I'm a bit drunk) vs 만취했어요 (very drunk) vs 꽐라 됐어 (slang: wasted). 취했어요 vs 취해요 — ONLY 취했어요 (past) correctly describes the current drunk state.
Degree scale: 살짝 취했어요 → 조금 취했어요 → 많이 취했어요 → 만취했어요 → 꽐라 됐어. Ongoing: 술기운이 오르고 있어요 ('the alcohol is coming up'). Seem: 취한 것 같아요 ('I think I'm drunk').

Two traps: (1) saying 안 취해요 (present) for 'I'm not drunk' — WRONG; the correct form uses the past: 안 취했어요, because 취하다 is a change-of-state verb where the past form = current condition. (2) Thinking a loud 안 취했어요! will convince people — paradoxically, loud denial is often a sign of intoxication.

mistakes: Saying 안 취해요 (present) for 'I'm not drunk'.
Korean uses past 취했어요 for the current drunk state. 'I'm not drunk' = 안 취했어요, not 안 취해요.
Treating 'drunk' as an English-style adjective.
There's no adjective 'drunk' to attach; use the verb 취하다 in past form: 취했어요 / 안 취했어요.
Confusing 취하다 (get drunk) with 취하다 (take a measure).
Same spelling, but with 술 it means intoxicated. 조치를 취하다 ('take action') is the other sense — context disambiguates.

usage: 반말, with friends the next day
어제 마신 게 아직도 안 깨요
Yesterday's drinks still haven't worn off
안 깨다 = the alcohol lingers; describes a stubborn morning-after feeling
My head feels like it's splitting
머리(가) 깨지다, vivid way to describe the headache component of a hangover
examples: 어제 과음했더니 숙취가 너무 심해요.
I overdrank yesterday, so my hangover is terrible.
과음하다 ('to drink too much', 過飮) is the cause; -더니 ('and as a result') is the cause-and-consequence connector
숙취 때문에 아침에 아무것도 못 먹었어요.
Because of the hangover, I couldn't eat anything this morning.
숙취 때문에 ('because of the hangover') as the cause of skipping breakfast — a very relatable real-life sentence

A: 어제 많이 마셨어요?
B: 네, 숙취가 심해서 죽겠어요. 해장국 먹으러 가요.

A: Did you drink a lot yesterday?
B: Yes, my hangover is killing me. Let's go get hangover soup.
숙취가 심해서 죽겠어요 ('so bad I could die') is a common hyperbolic complaint; immediately pivots to the remedy (해장국)
nuance: 숙취 (宿醉, 'lodged/leftover drunkenness') is the HANGOVER — the headache, nausea, fatigue, and brain fog the morning after drinking. 숙취가 심하다 = 'the hangover is severe'; 숙취가 있다 = 'to have a hangover'. The NOUN pattern is the grammar lesson: 숙취 takes subject markers 이/가 with descriptive adjectives — 숙취가 심하다, 숙취가 있다, 숙취가 없다 — and you cannot verb it as 숙취하다 (not a word). The most important contrast: 숙취 (the morning-after condition you suffer) vs 해장 (the ACT of eating to relieve it — hot soup, usually) — you HAVE 숙취 and you DO 해장 to cure it; conflating them is the most common learner mix-up. Also distinguish 숙취 (next-day aftermath) from 취하다 (being drunk during the drinking): 취했어요 is last night, 숙취 is this morning. The English-speaker pitfall: 'I'm hungover' has no adjective equivalent in Korean — you cannot say 나 hungover-해요; you must use the NOUN with predicates: 숙취가 있어요 / 심해요. Culturally relevant items: 숙취해소제 and 숙취해소음료 (hangover-relief pills and drinks sold at Korean convenience stores, often taken before or after drinking), 꿀물 (honey water), 헛개차 (hovenia tea, folk remedy), and 북엇국 / 콩나물국밥 / 선지해장국 (classic hangover soups).

structuredNuance.t: 숙취 = 宿醉, 'lodged/leftover drunkenness'. 숙취가 심해요 = 'the hangover is severe'. It is a NOUN, so you predicate it: 심해요, 있어요, 없어요. Do NOT try to say 나 숙취해 or 숙취됐어 — neither is Korean.

Used the morning after or the next day to explain your condition. With close friends/coworkers: 숙취 너무 심해, 죽겠어. Polite: 숙취가 좀 심해요. At the office: 어제 과음을 해서 좀 힘드네요 is softer if you don't want to say you're hung over bluntly.

숙취 (the hangover condition, noun) vs 해장 (the act of eating to relieve it, noun/verb) vs 과음 (overdrank, the CAUSE). The three form a causal chain: 과음하다 → 숙취가 생기다 → 해장하다. Knowing all three makes you sound naturally fluent in post-drinking conversation.
숙취 is Sino-Korean 宿醉 (宿 = lodge/overnight, 醉 = drunk). The 宿 (숙) character appears in 숙소 ('lodging'), so the image is 'drunkenness that lodged overnight in the body'.

Two traps: (1) trying to say 'I'm hungover' as an adjective — Korean has no such adjective; use the noun pattern: 숙취가 있어요 / 심해요; (2) mixing up 숙취 (the condition) and 해장 (the cure) — 해장국 is what you eat TO RELIEVE 숙취, not a synonym for it.

mistakes: Confusing 숙취 (hangover) with 취하다 (being drunk).
취했어요 = drunk now, during drinking. 숙취 = the aftermath the next day. 'I have a hangover' = 숙취가 있어요/심해요, not 취했어요.
Trying to say 숙취하다 as a verb.
숙취 is a noun and doesn't take 하다. Use it with 있다/심하다: 숙취가 있어요, 숙취가 심해요.
Mixing up 숙취 (the condition) with 해장 (the cure).
You HAVE 숙취 and you DO 해장 to fix it. 'My hangover is bad' = 숙취가 심해요; 'let's get hangover food' = 해장하러 가요.

nuance: 해장 (解酲, 'relieving the after-effects of drink') is the Korean morning-after ritual of eating a hot, brothy dish to recover from a hangover or the queasy stomach that follows. 해장하다 = 'cure a hangover by eating'; 해장국 is the soup itself (선지해장국, 콩나물국밥, 북엇국, 뚝배기 황태해장국). 해장하러 가요 uses -(으)러 가다 ('go in order to do ~'), the PURPOSE construction: you go FOR THE PURPOSE OF 해장. The near-synonym 속(을) 풀다 ('loosen/soothe the stomach') overlaps in feeling; 속 풀러 가요 is a slightly softer phrasing. The GRAMMAR TRAP is -(으)러 가다 vs -고 가다: 해장하러 가다 = 'go TO do 해장' (purpose); 해장하고 가다 = 'do 해장 and THEN go' (sequence) — different meanings. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: there is NO single English word for 해장 (it is not just 'hangover' — that is 숙취, the condition), so don't 직역. Second, conflating 숙취 (the hangover state) with 해장 (the remedy act): 숙취 있어요 = I have a hangover; 해장하러 가요 = let's go eat to cure it. Culturally, 해장 together is a bonding ritual — coworkers who drank at 회식 often go for 해장국 the next morning, and there is even 해장술 (a small 'hair-of-the-dog' drink), though that is its own debated custom. Knowing 해장 signals you understand the full drinking culture, not just the night itself.

structuredNuance.t: 해장 = 解酲, 'resolving/dispersing the after-effects of alcohol'. 해장하러 가요 = 'let's go for the purpose of doing 해장'. The key: 해장 is the ACT of eating to RELIEVE a hangover, not the hangover itself (that is 숙취). The two are complementary, not synonymous.

Propose 해장하러 가요 the morning after, usually when everyone is feeling rough. Polite: 해장하러 가요. Casual: 해장하러 가자. To ask what to eat: 해장국 뭐로 할까요? Classic spots: 해장국집, 김치찌개집, 순대국 식당. Note: 해장하러 가요 implies leaving to go somewhere; 해장하자 + ordering delivery is also fine.

해장하러 가요 (go to eat hangover food) vs 속 풀러 가요 (go to soothe the stomach — slightly softer image) vs 숙취가 심해요 (I have a bad hangover — the state, not the cure). These are three distinct moments: last night (취하다) → this morning (숙취) → the remedy (해장).

해장 is Sino-Korean 解酲 (解 = resolve/relieve, 酲 = the malaise from alcohol). The same 해 (解) character appears in 해결 ('solution') and 해소 ('relief/alleviation'), capturing the idea of 'resolving' the hangover state.

Two traps: (1) no English word covers 해장 precisely — 'hangover food' is the closest gloss, but 해장 is a verb AND a noun AND a cultural ritual; do not 직역 it as just 'hangover'; (2) the grammar -(으)러 가다 vs -고 가다: 해장하러 가요 = 'go TO eat'; 해장하고 가요 = 'eat first, THEN go'. Use -러 for purpose-of-going.

mistakes: Confusing 해장 (the cure-meal) with 숙취 (the hangover).
숙취 is the hangover condition; 해장 is the act of eating to relieve it. 'I have a hangover' = 숙취 있어요; 'let's get hangover food' = 해장하러 가요.
Using -고 가다 instead of -(으)러 가다 for purpose.
To say 'go in order to 해장', use -(으)러 가다: 해장하러 가요. 해장하고 가요 would mean 'do 해장 and then go', a different meaning.
Calling any post-drinking meal 해장 even without a hangover.
해장 specifically targets relieving drink after-effects. A normal next-day meal isn't necessarily 해장; the point is soothing the stomach/숙취.
